diagrams.title: Differential (Merz–Price) protection
diagrams.cap: The relay sees only the difference of the two CT currents. Percentage (biased) differential adds a restraint coil so CT mismatch on heavy through-faults does not cause a false trip.
diagrams.qq: Relay current for an external fault (ideal CTs)?

diagrams.title: Buchholz relay (gas-actuated) — transformer protection
diagrams.cap: Fitted in the pipe between the main tank and the conservator of oil-filled transformers above about 500 kVA. Gas from a small fault collects at the top and tilts the upper float (alarm); a big fault pushes an oil surge that tips the lower float (trip). It is the only relay that warns BEFORE a fault grows.
diagrams.qq: Which relay ANTICIPATES a major transformer fault?

diagrams.title: Distance relays on the R–X diagram (shaded = TRIP zone)
diagrams.cap: Impedance: trips if Z < set value in any direction (needs a separate directional unit). Reactance: trips if X < set value, not affected by fault (arc) resistance → short lines. Mho: circle through the origin, inherently directional and least affected by power swings → long lines.
diagrams.qq: Which distance relay is inherently directional?

diagrams.title: IDMT overcurrent relay: t = TMS × 0.14/(PSM^0.02 − 1)
diagrams.cap: Inverse at low multiples of the setting, definite minimum time at high multiples. Lower TMS shifts the whole curve down → faster. Grading: the relay nearer the source is set slower by ≈ 0.4 s.
diagrams.qq: TMS halved, same PSM. Operating time?

diagrams.title: Relay family tree (ANSI numbers in brackets)
diagrams.cap: Every relay = sensing element + comparison with a setting + output contact that trips the breaker through the trip coil. Numbers are the ANSI/IEEE device numbers often printed on drawings.
diagrams.qq: ANSI number of a differential relay?

diagrams.title: How a relay trips the circuit breaker (trip circuit)
diagrams.cap: The relay only CLOSES A CONTACT. The tripping energy comes from the station DC battery, because AC voltage may collapse during a fault. Total fault-clearing time = relay operating time + breaker opening (arcing) time.

diagrams.title: Induction-disc IDMT relay: what PS and TMS do
diagrams.cap: Plug setting decides at what current the relay starts (pickup = PS × CT secondary rating). TMS decides how long it takes (time = TMS × time from the curve).
diagrams.qq: Which setting changes the pickup current?

diagrams.title: Busbar protection — what senses what
diagrams.cap: All feeder CTs are paralleled into one relay (Kirchhoff's current law). A high-impedance relay stays stable even if one CT saturates on a heavy through fault.
diagrams.qq: Bus differential works on which law?
diagrams.qa: KCL: Σ currents = 0 for a healthy bus

diagrams.title: CT and PT connections
diagrams.cap: A CT goes in series with the line and feeds low-impedance current coils; a PT goes across the line and feeds high-impedance voltage coils. Open-circuiting a loaded CT secondary is dangerous; shorting a PT secondary is dangerous.
diagrams.qq: Why must a CT secondary never be opened on load?
diagrams.qa: Very high voltage appears across it

diagrams.title: Relay time grading, biased differential and directional relay
diagrams.cap: Graded relays trip nearest the fault first, each upstream relay waiting a margin. A biased differential relay trips only when the difference current exceeds a set fraction of the through current, and a directional relay trips only when the fault current lies in the forward half-plane.
diagrams.qq: Biased relay k = 10 %, I₁ = 10 A, I₂ = 9 A. Trip?

why.cause: fault current ↑ → IDMT relay trips faster
why.effect: Inverse time characteristic; PSM = I<sub>fault</sub>/(CT ratio × setting).

why.cause: distance relay: V/I = Z < setting → fault inside the zone → trips
SF₆: high dielectric strength + arc quenching → HV breakers
surge reaches an open end → Γ = +1 → voltage doubles
why.effect: That is why line ends and transformer terminals need lightning arresters.

why.cause: surge goes overhead line → cable (low Z) → τ small → voltage falls
why.effect: A short cable at the substation entry cuts the surge voltage.

why.cause: T = K₁I² + K₂V² + K₃VI cos(θ − τ): set one K = 0 → a different relay
why.effect: K₂ = 0 → reactance; K₃ = 0 → impedance; K₁ = 0 → mho.

why.cause: fault → CT current ↑ → relay torque > spring → contact closes → DC battery → trip coil → breaker opens
why.effect: The relay only senses and closes a contact; the breaker does the interrupting.

why.cause: plug setting ↑ → pickup current ↑ → PSM ↓ → relay slower
why.effect: TMS ↑ → time ↑ in direct proportion (t ∝ TMS).

mistakes.m: "Fuse current rating = the current at which it blows"
mistakes.c: Fusing current is higher than the rated current (fusing factor > 1).
Reactance relay = DIRECTIONAL-restrained overcurrent. Impedance = voltage-restrained overcurrent. Mho = voltage-restrained directional.

mistakes.m: A fuse and a circuit breaker do the same job
mistakes.c: A fuse acts once and must be replaced; a breaker can be reclosed and tripped remotely by relays.

ch.notes9: Rule: SHORT → current rises unless something collapses the field; OPEN → current stops, but an inductive winding (CT, field) can build a dangerous voltage. Memory trick: the word after 'restrained' is the OPERATING element. Impedance → current operates, voltage restrains. Reactance → current operates, directional restrains. Mho → directional operates, voltage restrains. Anticipating relay = Buchholz (gas). Fastest unit protection = differential. Distance relays: impedance (medium), reactance (short), mho (long). Distance zones: zone 1 ≈ 80–90 % of the line (instant), zone 2 ≈ 120 % (≈ 0.3–0.5 s), zone 3 ≈ next line + (≈ 1 s). Every relay only closes a contact → DC battery → trip coil → breaker opens. Lock-out relay (86) stops reclosing until reset by hand.

mcqs.q: Q1. A reactance relay is a
mcqs.ans: Ans: (b) Directional-restrained overcurrent relay T = K₁I² − K₃VI sin θ: current operates, directional element restrains (K₂ = 0).

mcqs.q: Q2. An impedance relay is a
mcqs.ans: Ans: (d) Voltage-restrained overcurrent relay T = K₁I² − K₂V² (K₃ = 0).

mcqs.q: Q3. A mho relay is a
mcqs.ans: Ans: (c) Voltage-restrained directional relay T = K₃VI cos(θ − τ) − K₂V² (K₁ = 0).

mcqs.q: Q4. In the universal relay torque equation, the VI cos(θ − τ) term represents the
mcqs.ans: Ans: (a) Directional element Product of V and I with a phase angle → direction.

mcqs.q: Q5. The relay whose R–X characteristic is a straight line parallel to the R axis is the
mcqs.ans: Ans: (a) Reactance relay Operates for X < K₁/K₃ regardless of R → not affected by arc resistance.

mcqs.q: Q6. Which relay can ANTICIPATE a major fault in a transformer?
mcqs.ans: Ans: (c) Buchholz relay Gas from an incipient fault collects and operates the alarm float before the fault grows.

mcqs.q: Q7. Buchholz relay is fitted
opts: (b) Between the main tank and the conservator
mcqs.ans: Ans: (b) Between the main tank and the conservator In the connecting pipe, so gas and oil surges pass through it.

mcqs.q: Q8. Negative-sequence relay protects an alternator against
mcqs.ans: Ans: (a) Unbalanced loading I₂ induces double-frequency currents in the rotor → heating.

mcqs.q: Q9. Reverse-power relay on a generator prevents
opts: (c) Motoring when the prime mover fails
mcqs.ans: Ans: (c) Motoring when the prime mover fails Generator would draw power and run as a motor.

mcqs.q: Q10. Over-fluxing relay responds to
mcqs.ans: Ans: (a) V/f ratio Flux ∝ V/f.

mcqs.q: Q11. Relay best suited for long EHV lines (least affected by power swings)
mcqs.ans: Ans: (c) Mho Smallest R–X area along the line angle.

mcqs.q: Q12. Translay relay is a
mcqs.ans: Ans: (d) Pilot-wire (unit) protection for feeders Compares both ends of a feeder over pilot wires.

mcqs.q: Q13. The trip coil of a circuit breaker is energised from
mcqs.ans: Ans: (b) Station DC battery AC may collapse during a fault; the battery is always available.

mcqs.q: Q14. Which relay setting changes the pickup current?
mcqs.ans: Ans: (a) Plug setting (PS) PS = current tap; TMS = time.

mcqs.q: Q15. TMS of an IDMT relay changed from 0.5 to 0.25. Operating time
mcqs.ans: Ans: (b) Halves t ∝ TMS.

mcqs.q: Q16. Total fault-clearing time equals
mcqs.ans: Ans: (a) Relay time + breaker time Relay closes its contact, then the breaker must open and quench the arc.

mcqs.q: Q17. Induction-disc relays cannot be used on
mcqs.ans: Ans: (b) DC They need two phase-displaced AC fluxes (T ∝ φ₁φ₂ sin θ).

mcqs.q: Q18. Extremely inverse relays are preferred for grading with
mcqs.ans: Ans: (b) Fuses Both follow an I²t-like characteristic.

mcqs.q: Q19. Zone 1 of a distance relay is usually set to
mcqs.ans: Ans: (d) 80–90 % of the line Avoids over-reach into the next section due to errors.

mcqs.q: Q20. In a Δ/Y transformer differential scheme, CTs on the star side are connected in
